newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish election budget expected to slash taxes.
newsitem.headline: Irish election budget expected to slash taxes.

text.p: Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, wooing workers in an election year, is expected to announce the first major cut in taxes for five years when he unveils his 1997 budget next Wednesday.

Quinn, who has overseen one of the strongest-growing economies in the European Union over the past two years, is tipped to cut one percentage point off both the the basic rate of income tax and pay-related social insurance (PRSI).
Reductions have been widely forecast by financial analysts and the media.
The poll faced by Prime Minister John Bruton's two-year-old right-left coalition government is not due until November.
But Bruton is expected to cash in on any "feelgood factor" generated by the budget to test the popularity of his three-party coalition in an early election, probably by May.

Government coffers are brimming with healthy tax returns and the economy has grown at an average rate of eight percent over the past two years, figures which have built up expectations that the public will be rewarded.
Analysts are forecasting income tax cuts of around 300 million punts ($493 million), including the first cut in the standard income tax rate since 1992.

Under the terms of a recent national pay agreement between government, employers and unions, the government has committed itself to tax reductions of one billion punts on a full-year basis over a three-year period.

"On the tax side, we assume that about a third of the one billion punts in tax reductions agreed in the national agreement will be delivered," Dermot O'Brien, economist at NCB Stockbrokers, told Reuters.
"If anything the numbers might be a bit higher at the end of the day. There's been talk of frontloading but nobody's put an actual number on it," he said.

The standard rate of personal income tax is expected to be cut to 26 percent from 27 percent, while Quinn is also tipped to raise personal allowances and cut employees' pay-related social insurance (PRSI) by a percentage point to 4.5 percent.
"It's all part of a general move toward a standard tax rate of 25 percent and a top rate of tax of 40 percent," one accountant said.
Quinn is also expected to have some good news for the business community.

Most analysts expect him to follow last year's two percentage point cut in corporation tax with a further reduction, taking the rate to 36 percent from the current 38 percent. He may also lower the threshold at which employers' PRSI is payable, analysts say.

The budget is unlikely to have much impact on indirect taxes as Quinn avoids putting upward pressure on inflation in a year in which Ireland has to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union, they add.
While he is likely to follow the pattern of recent years by increasing excise taxes on cigarettes, many analysts believe he may leave alcohol and petrol alone.

"If the minister is worried about the inflation rate in 1997, in the context of having a sufficiently low rate of inflation to qualify for the single currency, he may reduce indirect taxes slightly. But this does not appear likely at this stage," Eoin Fahy, economist at Ulster Bank Markets, said.
